title: Design Twitter
problem: Design a simplified Twitter. Users can post tweets, follow and unfollow other users, and fetch their news feed. getNewsFeed(userId) returns the 10 most recent tweet ids posted by the user or by anyone they follow, newest first.
example: Explanation: User 1 posts 5 and sees [5]. After following user 2, who posts 6, user 1 sees [6,5].
intuition: "Most recent" means we need a global clock: every tweet gets an increasing timestamp. Each user's own tweets are naturally sorted by time if we append them to a list. So a news feed is really: "I have several sorted lists (one per followee plus myself); give me the 10 largest timestamps across all of them". That is exactly merge K sorted lists, and the tool for it is a heap. Put the newest tweet of each relevant user into a max-heap (by time). Pop the top: it is the newest tweet overall. Then push the next older tweet of that same user. After 10 pops we are done. We never touch tweets that cannot be in the top 10.
notes: Say it like this: "The naive design keeps one global tweet list and scans backwards for each feed, which is O(total tweets) per feed. Instead I store each user's tweets in time order and treat the feed as merging K sorted lists: a max-heap seeded with each followee's newest tweet gives the top 10 in O(F + 10 log F)."
Edge cases: user with no tweets and no followees (empty feed); following yourself (the set handles duplicates); unfollowing someone you never followed; fewer than 10 tweets in total.

Common mistakes: forgetting to include the user's own tweets; using the tweet id as the timestamp (ids are not ordered by time); allowing the user to unfollow themselves and then losing their own tweets (we always add self at feed time, so it is safe).

Follow-ups: "Millions of users?" Fan-out on write (push tweet ids into each follower's feed cache) for normal users and fan-out on read (this heap merge) for celebrities. "Memory?" Only the last 10 tweets per user can ever appear in a feed, so lists can be capped at 10. 8.2
simple: Build a mini Twitter: post, follow, unfollow, and show the 10 newest tweets from you and people you follow.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Keep one global list of all tweets (userId, tweetId) in posting order, and a map follower -> set of followees.
For a feed, scan the global list from the end and collect tweets whose author is the user or a followee, stopping at 10.
approaches.time: O(T) per getNewsFeed , O(1) for the rest
approaches.why: In the worst case we scan every tweet ever posted (T) because the user follows nobody active; F is the number of follow relations stored.
approaches.simple: Keep one global list of all tweets and scan it from newest, keeping those from followed users.

approaches.label: Optimal (Per-user lists + max-heap merge)
steps: Keep a global counter time. Each user has a list of {time, tweetId}; posting appends (so each list is sorted by time).
For a feed, collect the set of users = followees + self. For each, push its last tweet into a max-heap keyed by time, together with the user id and the index in that user's list.
Pop up to 10 times. After popping (user, idx), push (user, idx - 1) if it exists.
approaches.time: O(F + 10 log F) per getNewsFeed , where F = number of followees; O(1) for post/follow/unfollow
approaches.why: Building the heap touches each followee once; then only 10 pops and at most 10 pushes on a heap of size at most F + 1.
approaches.simple: Each user keeps their own tweets. To build the feed, merge the newest tweets of followed users with a max-heap.

title: Find Median From Data Stream
problem: Design a class that receives numbers one at a time (addNum) and can return the median of all numbers seen so far (findMedian) at any moment. With an even count, the median is the average of the two middle values.
example: Explanation: After 1,2 the middle values are 1 and 2, median 1.5. After 1,2,3 the middle is 2.
intuition: The median only cares about the boundary between the smaller half and the larger half. We do not need the halves sorted, we only need the largest of the small half and the smallest of the large half. That is exactly what a max-heap and a min-heap give us at the top.

Keep small (max-heap) and large (min-heap) with two rules: every element of small is ≤ every element of large, and small has either the same size as large or one more. Then the median is small.top (odd count) or the average of both tops (even count). To insert while keeping both rules: push into small, move small 's top into large (this fixes the ordering rule), and if large became bigger, move its top back into small (this fixes the size rule). Trace with 1, 2, 3: add 1 → small=[1]. Add 2 → small=[2,1] → move 2 → large=[2], small=[1]. Add 3 → small=[3,1] → move 3 → large=[2,3] is bigger → move 2 back → small=[2,1], large=[3]. Median = 2.
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force sorts on every query, O(n log n); keeping a sorted list makes the query O(1) but insertion O(n) because of shifting. With a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, kept balanced, insertion is O(log n) and the median is just the tops, O(1)."
Edge cases: negative numbers; duplicates; even vs odd count; sum of two large ints overflowing (cast to long in Java).

Common mistakes: pushing directly into one heap based on a comparison and forgetting to rebalance; allowing large to be the bigger heap and then reading the wrong top; integer division (a + b) / 2 instead of / 2.0.

Follow-ups: "All numbers are in [0, 100]?" Keep a count array of size 101 and walk it to the middle, O(100) per query. "99% in [0, 100]?" Count array plus two counters/lists for outliers below and above. "Sliding window median?" Two heaps with lazy deletion, or two TreeMap s/multisets. 8.3
simple: Numbers keep arriving; at any time give the median.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Append every number to a list.
On findMedian, sort the list and read the middle.
approaches.time: addNum O(1), findMedian O(n log n)
approaches.why: Every median query re-sorts all n numbers.
approaches.simple: Store everything and sort when asked.

approaches.label: Better (Keep the list sorted)
steps: Keep the list always sorted: binary search the insert position and insert there.
findMedian reads the middle directly.
approaches.why: Binary search is O(log n), but inserting into the middle of an array shifts up to n elements.
approaches.simple: Keep the list sorted by inserting each number in its correct place.

approaches.label: Optimal (Two heaps)
steps: small = max-heap (lower half), large = min-heap (upper half).
addNum: push into small; pop small 's top into large; if large.size() > small.size(), pop large 's top back into small.
findMedian: if sizes differ, small.top; else average of both tops.
approaches.why: Each add does a constant number of heap pushes/pops (O(log n) each); the median is read from the two tops.
approaches.simple: Two heaps: a max-heap for the smaller half and a min-heap for the larger half. The median sits on their tops.

title: K Closest Points to Origin
problem: Given an array of points [x, y] and an integer k, return the k points closest to the origin (0, 0) by Euclidean distance. The answer can be in any order.
example: Explanation: Squared distances are 18, 26, 20. The two smallest are 18 and 20.
intuition: First, never take the square root: comparing x² + y² gives the same order as comparing the real distances, and stays in integers.

Then it is a top-K problem. Sorting all n points does more work than needed; we only need the k smallest. Keep a max-heap of size k: the top is the farthest of the current k best. When a new point comes, push it; if the heap grows past k, pop the top (the farthest). What remains at the end is the k closest. The heap is "max" because the element we want to throw away is the largest distance.
notes: Say it like this: "Sorting by squared distance is O(n log n). Since I only need k points, a max-heap capped at size k keeps the k closest seen so far, giving O(n log k) time and O(k) space. Quickselect can do it in O(n) average if they want better."
Edge cases: k equals n (return everything); ties in distance (any is fine); negative coordinates (squaring handles it).

Common mistakes: using a min-heap of all n points and popping k times (works, but O(n + k log n) and O(n) space, and people often forget that it is not the "size-k" trick); using Math.sqrt and doubles; overflow is not an issue here since coordinates are ≤ 10⁴ (sum ≤ 2·10⁸).
Follow-ups: "Do it in O(n)?" Quickselect on distance (average O(n), worst O(n²); random pivot). "Points arrive as a stream?" The size-k heap already works for a stream. 8.4
simple: Find the k points closest to (0, 0).

approaches.label: Brute Force (Sort)
steps: Sort all points by x² + y².
Return the first k.
approaches.space: O(n) (or O(log n) for the sort's own stack)
approaches.why: Sorting all n points dominates.
approaches.simple: Sort all points by distance and take k.

approaches.label: Optimal (Max-heap of size k)
steps: For each point, push it into a max-heap ordered by squared distance.
If the heap size exceeds k, pop the top (farthest).
The heap now holds the k closest points.
approaches.why: Each of n points costs at most one push and one pop on a heap capped at k + 1 elements.
approaches.simple: Keep a max-heap of the k closest so far; throw out the farthest when it grows past k.

title: Kth Largest Element In An Array
problem: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the k-th largest element in sorted order (not the k-th distinct element). Try to do better than sorting.
example: Explanation: Sorted descending: 6,5,4,3,2,1. The 2nd largest is 5.
intuition: The k-th largest is the element that would sit at index n - k if the array were sorted ascending. Sorting gets there in O(n log n) but sorts much more than we need.

Heap idea: keep the k largest seen so far in a min-heap. The top is the smallest of those k, i.e. the k-th largest so far. Any new number smaller than the top cannot be in the top k; a larger one replaces the top.

Quickselect idea: quicksort's partition puts one pivot into its final sorted position and splits the rest into "smaller" and "larger". If the pivot lands at index n - k, we are done. Otherwise we only recurse into the one side that contains index n - k, so the work is n + n/2 + n/4 +... ≈ 2n on average.
notes: Say it like this: "Sorting is O(n log n). A min-heap of size k keeps the k largest and gives O(n log k) with O(k) space, which is what I'd use for a stream. For a fixed array, quickselect with a random pivot is O(n) on average and O(1) extra space; I use a three-way partition so duplicates don't make it quadratic."
Edge cases: k = 1 (maximum), k = n (minimum), all elements equal, negative numbers.

Common mistakes: using a max-heap and popping k times (O(n + k log n), fine but not the intended trick); off-by- one between "k-th largest" and index n - k; Lomuto partition with a fixed last-element pivot (TLE on sorted or all-equal input).

Follow-ups: "Guaranteed O(n) worst case?" Median of medians (rarely coded in interviews, just mention it). "Values are in a small range (e.g. -10⁴..10⁴)?" Counting sort: count array, walk from the top until k elements are covered, O(n + range). "Does quickselect modify the input?" Yes; copy it first if that matters. 8.5

approaches.label: Brute Force (Sort)
steps: Sort ascending.
Return nums[n - k].
approaches.why: Full sort of n elements.
approaches.simple: Sort and pick.

approaches.label: Better (Min-heap of size k)
steps: Push each number into a min-heap.
If the size exceeds k, pop the smallest.
The top is the answer.
approaches.why: Each push/pop is O(log k) on a heap capped at k + 1.
approaches.simple: Keep a min-heap of the k largest so far; its top is the answer.

approaches.label: Optimal (Quickselect with 3-way partition)
steps: target = n - k (index in ascending order). Work on the range [lo, hi], initially the whole array.
Pick a random pivot. Partition the range into three parts: < pivot, == pivot, > pivot (Dutch national flag). Let the equal block be [lt, gt].
If target < lt, continue in the left part; if target > gt, continue in the right part; otherwise the pivot is the answer.
approaches.why: Each round scans the current range and keeps only one side, so the expected total is n + n/2 +... ≈ 2n. A random pivot makes the O(n²) case extremely unlikely, and the 3-way partition keeps arrays with many duplicates linear (a plain Lomuto partition degrades to O(n²) when all values are equal).
approaches.simple: Quickselect: split around a pivot and only keep searching in the part that contains the k-th position.

title: Kth Largest Element In a Stream
problem: Design a class KthLargest(k, nums) that starts with an initial array, and whose method add(val) inserts a new score and returns the k-th largest score among all scores so far.
example: Explanation: After adding 3 the scores are 2,3,4,5,8 -> 3rd largest is 4. After 5: 2,3,4,5,5,8 -> 5.
intuition: Numbers only ever get added, never removed. Once a number has fallen below the k-th largest, it can never come back into the top k (adding things only pushes the k-th largest up). So we only need to remember the k largest numbers. Store them in a min-heap; its top is the k-th largest. On add, push and, if size > k, pop the smallest.
notes: Say it like this: "A sorted list works but each insert is O(n). Because numbers are only added, anything below the current k-th largest is dead forever, so I keep just the k largest in a min-heap: O(log k) per add and O(k) memory."
Edge cases: initial array shorter than k (LeetCode guarantees there will be k elements by the time you query, so the heap just fills up); duplicates; negative values.
Common mistakes: using a max-heap; not trimming the initial array to k; returning pq.peek() before trimming.
Follow-ups: "What if numbers can also be removed?" A heap can no longer drop the right element cheaply; use two TreeMap s (top-k and the rest) or an order-statistics tree. 8.6
simple: Numbers stream in; after each one, report the k-th largest so far.

approaches.label: Brute Force (Sorted list)
steps: Keep all numbers in a sorted list.
On add, binary search the position and insert, then return the element at index size - k.
approaches.time: O(n) per add (O(n log n) to set up)
approaches.why: Inserting into the middle of an array shifts up to n elements, and we keep every number ever added.
approaches.simple: Keep a sorted list and read position k from the end.

approaches.label: Optimal (Min-heap of size k)
steps: Push all initial numbers into a min-heap, popping whenever size > k.
On add(val): push val; if size > k, pop. Return the top.
approaches.time: O(n log k) setup, O(log k) per add
approaches.why: The heap never holds more than k + 1 elements.
approaches.simple: Keep a min-heap of size k; its top is always the k-th largest.

title: Last Stone Weight
problem: You have stones with positive weights. Each turn, take the two heaviest stones x ≤ y and smash them: if equal, both are destroyed; otherwise the lighter is destroyed and the heavier becomes y - x. Return the weight of the last remaining stone, or 0 if none remain.
intuition: The rule is "repeatedly take the two largest and maybe put a new value back". Any time you repeatedly need the current maximum while inserting new values, that is a max-heap. There is no clever formula to find here; the point is to make each step O(log n) instead of re-sorting.
notes: Say it like this: "Re-sorting every round is O(n² log n). Since each step needs the two largest and may insert one value, a max-heap makes each step O(log n), so O(n log n) total with O(n) space."
Edge cases: one stone (return it); all stones cancel (return 0).
Common mistakes: Java's PriorityQueue is a min-heap by default, so forgetting Collections.reverseOrder(); pushing back a 0 when stones are equal (harmless here but wasteful, and wrong in variants).

Follow-ups: "Weights are small (≤ 1000)?" Bucket counts by weight and walk from the top, O(n + maxWeight). "Last Stone Weight II (smash any two)?" Totally different: it becomes a subset-sum DP that splits stones into two groups with minimum difference. 8.7
simple: Smash the two heaviest stones each turn; what weight is left at the end?

approaches.label: Brute Force (Sort every round)
steps: While at least two stones remain, sort the list.
Remove the two largest; if they differ, add their difference back.
approaches.why: Up to n rounds (each round removes at least one stone), and each round sorts O(n log n).
approaches.simple: Sort every round and take the two biggest.

approaches.label: Optimal (Max-heap)
steps: Put all stones in a max-heap.
While size > 1: pop y, pop x; if y!= x, push y - x.
Return the top, or 0 if empty.
approaches.why: At most n rounds, each with a constant number of O(log n) heap operations.
approaches.simple: A max-heap hands you the two biggest instantly each round.

title: Task Scheduler
problem: Given CPU tasks labelled 'A' to 'Z' and a cooldown n, each unit of time the CPU either runs one task or stays idle. Two runs of the same task must be at least n units apart. Return the minimum number of time units needed to finish all tasks.
example: Explanation: A -> B -> idle -> A -> B -> idle -> A -> B. Identical tasks are 3 slots apart.
intuition: Only the counts matter, not the letters. The task with the highest count is the bottleneck: it creates "frames". If A occurs maxF times, we need maxF - 1 full frames of length n + 1 (A followed by n other slots), plus a final partial frame that holds A and every other task that also occurs maxF times. So:
frames = (maxF - 1) * (n + 1) + countOfTasksWithMaxF.

Other tasks fill the idle slots in the frames. If there are so many tasks that they overflow the frames, there is no idle time at all and the answer is simply tasks.length. So the answer is max(tasks.length, frames). Example: maxF = 3 (A and B), n = 2 → (3-1)·3 + 2 = 8.

If you cannot see the formula in an interview, the greedy simulation is also accepted: at each time unit run the available task with the most remaining copies (it is the one most likely to cause idle time later).
notes: Say it like this: "A greedy simulation that always runs the available task with the most remaining copies works; with a max-heap and a cooldown queue it is O(total time). But the most frequent task fixes the structure: (maxF - 1) frames of size n + 1 plus the tasks tied for max frequency, and if there are more tasks than slots there is no idle at all. That gives max(N, (maxF-1)(n+1) + maxCount) in O(N)."
Edge cases: n = 0 (answer is N); one task type (answer (maxF-1)(n+1)+1); many distinct tasks (answer N).

Common mistakes: forgetting the max with tasks.length; forgetting that several tasks can share maxF; in the simulation, picking any available task instead of the one with the highest count (that greedy is wrong).

Follow-ups: "Return an actual schedule?" Use the heap + queue simulation and record what runs each unit. "Tasks must run in the given order (Task Scheduler II)?" Then it is a simple pass with a map task -> next allowed day. 8.8
simple: Run tasks with a cooldown of n between the same task. What is the least total time?

approaches.label: Brute Force (Time-step simulation)
steps: Count each task; keep next[c] = earliest time task c may run again.
For each time unit, scan the 26 letters and run the available one with the highest remaining count (or idle if none is available).
Stop when all tasks are done.
approaches.time: O(T · 26), where T is the answer (at most tasks.length · (n + 1) )
approaches.why: Each time unit scans 26 letters; the arrays have fixed size 26.
approaches.simple: Simulate time step by step, choosing a ready task each tick.

approaches.label: Better (Max-heap + cooldown queue)
steps: Push all non-zero counts into a max-heap.
Each time unit: pop the largest count, decrement it, and if still > 0 put (count, readyTime = time + n) in a FIFO queue.
If the queue's front is ready at this time, move it back into the heap. Continue until both are empty.
approaches.why: Same number of time steps as the simulation, but choosing the next task is a heap operation on at most 26 items. This is the version NeetCode teaches and it generalises to "also output the schedule".
approaches.simple: Always run the task with the most copies left (max-heap) and park it in a waiting queue during its cooldown.

approaches.label: Optimal (Counting formula)
steps: Count frequencies; let maxF be the highest and maxCount the number of tasks with that frequency.
Answer = max(tasks.length, (maxF - 1) * (n + 1) + maxCount).
approaches.why: One pass to count, one pass over 26 letters.
approaches.simple: The most frequent task sets the frame: (maxF − 1) gaps of size n + 1, plus the tasks that tie for maxF. The answer is that or the number of tasks, whichever is bigger.

title: Heapify Algorithm
problem: You are given an array nums that is a valid min-heap (stored the usual way: children of index i are 2i+1 and 2i+2), and two integers ind and val. Set nums[ind] = val and then rearrange the array so that it is a valid min-heap again. Modify the array in place.
example: Explanation: After the update the array is [1,4,5,5,7,2]. Index 5 (value 2) is smaller than its parent
index 2 (value 5), so swap -> [1,4,2,5,7,5]. Index 2 (value 2) vs parent index 0 (value 1): fine, stop.
intuition: A min-heap has one rule: every parent ≤ its children. Changing a single value can only break that rule around that one node:

If the new value is smaller than before, it might now be smaller than its parent. Its children are still fine (they were ≥ the old, larger value). So bubble it up: swap with the parent while it is smaller. If the new value is larger, it might now be larger than a child. The parent is still fine. So push it down: swap with the smaller child while it is larger than that child.

Each move goes one level, and a heap of n elements has about log₂ n levels. This "fix one spot" routine is called heapify, and it is the building block of every heap operation (insert = sift up, remove top = sift down, build heap = sift down many times).
notes: Say it like this: "Sorting after the update gives a valid heap in O(n log n), but only one node changed. If the value decreased it can only violate the rule with its parent, so I sift up; if it increased it can only violate with its children, so I sift down towards the smaller child. Either way it is one path, O(log n)."
Edge cases: ind is the root (only sift down possible); ind is a leaf (only sift up possible); val equals the old value (nothing moves); a node with only a left child.

Common mistakes: swapping with the larger child when sifting down in a min-heap (breaks the rule between the two siblings); using i / 2 as the parent (that is for 1-indexed heaps; 0-indexed is (i-1)/2); checking r < n but forgetting l < n.
Follow-ups: "Max-heap version?" Flip every comparison. "Why swap with the smaller child?" The smaller child becomes the parent of the other child, so the rule holds between them automatically. 8.9
simple: One value in a min-heap changes. Fix the heap.

approaches.label: Brute Force (Update, then rebuild by sorting)
steps: Set nums[ind] = val.
Sort the array. A sorted ascending array is always a valid min-heap (every parent index is smaller than its children's indices, so its value is ≤ theirs).
approaches.why: We throw away the existing heap structure and fix everything instead of one path.
extra: Note: the judge may compare against the exact array produced by sift up/down. Sorting gives a valid heap but not necessarily the same one, so use this only as a stepping stone.
approaches.simple: Change it and just sort the whole array.

approaches.label: Optimal (Sift up or sift down from ind )
steps: Remember old = nums[ind], then set nums[ind] = val.
If val < old: sift up. While i > 0 and nums[i] < nums[(i-1)/2], swap with the parent and move up.
Else: sift down. Find the smaller child; if it is smaller than nums[i], swap and move down; stop otherwise.
approaches.why: Only one root-to-leaf path is touched, and its length is the height of the heap, ⌊log₂ n⌋.
approaches.simple: If the new value got smaller, bubble it up; if bigger, push it down.

title: Build heap from a given Array
problem: Given an unsorted array nums, rearrange it in place so that it becomes a valid min-heap (parent ≤ children, children of i at 2i+1 and 2i+2).
example: Explanation: Sift down index 2 (2 <= 7, no change), index 1 (5 swaps with 1 -> [6,1,2,7,5,7]),
index 0 (6 swaps with 1 -> [1,6,2,7,5,7], then 6 swaps with 5 -> [1,5,2,7,6,7]).
intuition: Leaves (the second half of the array, indices n/2.. n-1) are already valid heaps of size 1. If we process the internal nodes from the last one (n/2 - 1) back to the root, then whenever we reach a node, both of its subtrees are already valid heaps. Sifting this node down then makes its whole subtree valid. When we reach the root, the whole array is a heap.

Why is this O(n) and not O(n log n)? A sift down costs the height of the node, not log n. Half the nodes are leaves (cost 0), a quarter have height 1, an eighth height 2, and so on: n/4·1 + n/8·2 + n/16·3 +... = n · Σ h/2^(h+1) < n. Most of the work happens on the many short subtrees near the bottom, and only one node (the root) pays the full log n.
notes: Say it like this: "Inserting elements one by one with sift up is O(n log n). Building bottom-up, sifting down every internal node from the last one to the root, is O(n), because the cost is the node's height and most nodes are near the bottom. This is exactly what PriorityQueue(Collection) and heap sort's first phase do."
Edge cases: empty array or one element (loop does not run); already a heap (no swaps); all equal values.

Common mistakes: iterating from the root downwards with sift down (does not work, the subtrees are not heaps yet); starting the loop at n/2 (harmless, it is a leaf) or at n/2 - 2 (misses a node); claiming O(n log n) for the bottom-up method.

Follow-ups: "Heap sort?" Build a max-heap in O(n), then repeatedly swap the root with the last element and sift down on the shrinking prefix: O(n log n), O(1) space, not stable. "Check whether an array is a min-heap?" For every i < n/2, check a[i] <= a[2i+1] and a[i] <= a[2i+2] when that child exists, O(n). 8.10
simple: Turn an array into a min-heap.

approaches.label: Brute Force (Insert one by one, sift up)
steps: Treat nums[0..0] as a heap.
For i = 1.. n-1, "insert" nums[i] by sifting it up into the heap nums[0..i].
approaches.why: Each of n inserts can climb the full height log n (e.g. a descending input makes every element climb to the root).
approaches.simple: Insert elements one at a time, bubbling each up.

approaches.label: Optimal (Bottom-up sift down)
steps: For i = n/2 - 1 down to 0, sift nums[i] down (swap with the smaller child while larger than it).
approaches.why: The cost of each sift down is the node's height, and the sum of heights over all nodes is less than n (see Intuition).
approaches.simple: Start from the last parent and push each parent down into place, moving to the front. This takes only O(n).

title: Implement Min Heap
problem: Implement a min-heap class supporting: initializeHeap() (start empty), insert(key), changeKey(index, newVal) (change the value at array position index), extractMin() (remove the minimum; here we also return it), isEmpty(), getMin(), and heapSize(). Do not use the language's built-in priority queue.
example: Explanation: After inserting 4,1,10 the heap array is [1,4,10]. extractMin removes 1 -> [4,10].
changeKey(0,16) sets 4 to 16 and sifts it down -> [10,16], so getMin is 10.
intuition: A heap is just an array plus two repair routines from 8.8:

insert: append at the end (keeps the shape a complete tree), then sift up. extractMin: the minimum is at index 0. Move the last element to index 0, shrink the array, then sift down from 0. (Removing the root directly would leave a hole in the middle of the tree.) changeKey: set the value; sift up if it decreased, sift down if it increased. getMin, isEmpty, heapSize: read the array.
notes: Say it like this: "An unsorted list gives O(1) insert but O(n) getMin and extractMin. A binary heap stored in an array keeps the minimum at index 0: insert appends and sifts up, extractMin moves the last element to the root and sifts down, and changeKey sifts in whichever direction the value moved. All updates are O(log n) and getMin is O(1)."
Edge cases: extracting from a heap with one element (do not write the removed last element back into an empty array); changeKey on the root or a leaf; duplicate values.
Common mistakes: removing index 0 with list.remove(0) (O(n) shift and it breaks the tree shape); forgetting the empty check after removing the last element; always sifting down in changeKey.

Follow-ups: "Decrease-key by value, not index (for Dijkstra)?" Keep a map value/id -> index and update it on every swap. "Generic heap?" Use a Comparator<T> instead of <. "Merge two heaps fast?" Binary heaps merge in O(n) by rebuilding; leftist/binomial/Fibonacci heaps merge faster. 8.11
simple: Build a min-heap by hand: insert, get min, remove min, change a key.

approaches.label: Brute Force (Unsorted list)
steps: Store values in an unsorted list.
insert and changeKey are direct writes; getMin and extractMin scan the whole list for the minimum.
approaches.time: insert / changeKey O(1), getMin / extractMin O(n)
approaches.why: Without any ordering, finding the minimum requires looking at every element. (The index meaning of changeKey is "position in our list", which is consistent within this implementation.)
approaches.simple: Keep an unsorted list and scan for the minimum when needed.

approaches.label: Optimal (Binary heap in an array)
steps: Store the heap in an array list a.
insert: append and sift up. extractMin: save a[0], move the last element to 0, remove the last slot, sift down from 0.
changeKey: write the value, then sift up or down depending on whether it decreased or increased.
approaches.time: insert , extractMin , changeKey O(log n); getMin , isEmpty , heapSize O(1)
approaches.why: Every update walks at most one root-to-leaf path of length log n.
approaches.simple: Keep a real binary heap in an array: children of i are 2i+1 and 2i+2; bubble up on insert and push down on removal.

title: Implement Trie Prefix Tree
problem: Implement a Trie class with insert(word), search(word) (is this exact word stored?) and startsWith(prefix) (is any stored word starting with this prefix?). Words use lowercase letters only.
example: Explanation: "app" is only a prefix until it is inserted as a word itself.
intuition: Words that share a prefix should share storage. Picture a tree whose edges are letters: from the root, following a -> p -> p reaches the node that represents the prefix "app". Inserting "apple" creates the path a,p,p,l,e; inserting "app" afterwards creates nothing new, it only marks the node at the end of a,p,p as "a word ends here".

So each node needs two things: up to 26 child links and an isEnd flag. search walks the path and checks isEnd at the end; startsWith only checks that the path exists. Both cost O(length) regardless of how many words are stored. That independence from the number of words is the whole point of a trie.
notes: Say it like this: "With a hash set, search is O(L) but a prefix query has to scan all N words. A trie stores shared prefixes once; each node has 26 child links and an end-of-word flag, so insert, search and startsWith are all O(L), independent of how many words are stored."
Edge cases: searching a prefix that exists but was never inserted as a word ("app" before inserting it); inserting the same word twice; empty string (if allowed, the root's isEnd).
Common mistakes: search returning true just because the path exists (forgetting isEnd); creating nodes inside search; sharing one children array across nodes by accident.

Follow-ups: "Unicode or large alphabet?" Use a HashMap<Character, Node> per node instead of an array (less memory for sparse nodes, a bit slower). "Delete a word?" Unset isEnd and remove nodes bottom-up that have no children and are not ends (or keep a prefix counter, see 8.14). "Autocomplete top 3?" Store at each node the best suggestions, or DFS from the prefix node. 8.12
simple: Build a trie: insert words, search a word, check if any word starts with a prefix.

approaches.label: Brute Force (Hash set + scan)
steps: Store words in a HashSet.
search is a set lookup. startsWith loops over every stored word and checks word.startsWith(prefix).
approaches.time: insert / search O(L), startsWith O(N · L)
approaches.why: Hashing a word costs its length L; a prefix query must look at all N words.
approaches.simple: Keep words in a set; for prefixes, check every word.

approaches.label: Optimal (Trie with 26 children per node)
steps: Node = children[26] + isEnd.
insert: walk from the root, creating missing children; mark the last node isEnd = true.
search: walk; if a child is missing return false; at the end return isEnd. startsWith: same walk, return true if the path exists.
approaches.space: O(total characters · 26) in the worst case
approaches.why: Each operation touches one node per character; each new character may create a node with a 26-slot array.
approaches.simple: A tree of letters. Each step down follows one letter; a star marks where a word ends.

title: Design Add And Search Words Data Structure
problem: Design WordDictionary with addWord(word) and search(word). In search, the pattern may contain. which matches any single letter. Return whether any added word matches the whole pattern.
example: Explanation: "pad" was never added. ".ad" matches bad/dad/mad, "b.." matches bad.
intuition: Without dots this is exactly the trie from 8.11. A dot means "this letter could be anything", so at that node we cannot pick one child, we must try every existing child and succeed if any branch matches the rest of the pattern. That is a DFS over the trie: dfs(node, i) = can the pattern from index i be matched starting at node?
Real letters keep the search on a single path, so it stays fast; only dots fan out, and they only fan out into children that actually exist.
notes: Say it like this: "Scanning all stored words is O(N·L) per search. In a trie, letters follow a single path; for a dot I branch into every existing child with DFS. Without dots search is O(L); with d dots the worst case is 26^d paths, which is small because the problem allows at most two dots."
Edge cases: pattern of only dots (matches any word of that length); pattern longer than any word; a prefix of a stored word ("ba" when only "bad" exists must be false).
Common mistakes: returning true when the path exists but isEnd is false; returning the first branch's result for a dot instead of trying all branches; creating nodes during search.

Follow-ups: "Support * (any sequence)?" DFS gets a choice to consume zero or more characters at each node, like wildcard matching on a trie. "Many dots?" Bucket words by length first, so a pattern only compares with words of its own length. 8.13
simple: Add words and search patterns where . matches any letter.

approaches.label: Brute Force (List of words)
steps: Store every added word in a list.
For search, compare the pattern with each word of the same length, character by character, treating. as a match.
approaches.why: Every search compares against all N stored words.
approaches.simple: Compare the pattern against every stored word of the same length.

approaches.label: Optimal (Trie + DFS on dots)
steps: addWord: normal trie insert.
search: dfs(node, i). If i == length, return node.isEnd. If pattern[i] is a letter, go to that child (fail if missing). If it is., try dfs(child, i + 1) for every non-null child.
approaches.time: addWord O(L); search O(L) without dots, O(26^d · L) worst case with d dots
approaches.space: O(total characters · 26) for the trie, O(L) recursion
approaches.why: Letters follow one path; each dot can branch into up to 26 children. LeetCode limits patterns to at most 2 dots, so this is fast in practice.
approaches.simple: Store words in a trie. A dot tries every child branch; a letter follows just one.

title: Word Search II
problem: Given an m x n board of letters and a list of words, return all words that can be formed by a path of horizontally or vertically adjacent cells, using each cell at most once per word. Return them in any order.
example: Explanation: "oath" goes o(0,0) a(0,1) t(1,1) h(2,1); "eat" goes e(1,3) a(1,2) t(1,1).
intuition: Running Word Search I once per word repeats the same exploration again and again: "oath" and "oat" and "oak" all start by walking o -> a. Flip the loop around: put all words into a trie, then do one DFS from every cell, walking the board and the trie together. At each step we move to the trie child for the current letter. If that child does not exist, no word continues this way, so we stop immediately; this is the pruning that makes it fast. When we reach a trie node that ends a word, we record it. Two practical tricks: store the full word at its end node (so we don't have to rebuild it from the path), and set it to null once found so the same word is not reported twice. Optionally delete trie leaves after use, which shrinks the trie as words are found and speeds up later searches.
notes: Say it like this: "Running Word Search I for every word costs W times the grid DFS. Instead I build a trie of all the words and do one backtracking DFS from each cell, walking the trie alongside; a missing trie child cuts the branch immediately. That removes the W factor: O(m·n·4·3^(L-1)) worst case, and pruning found words keeps it fast."
Edge cases: duplicate words in the input; a word that is a prefix of another ("oa" and "oath", both must be found, so do not return after finding the first); 1x1 board; words longer than m·n.

Common mistakes: stopping the DFS after finding a word (longer words through the same path are lost); reporting a word twice (forgetting word = null or a set); forgetting to restore the cell after the DFS; building the string along the path (slow) instead of storing it in the node.

Follow-ups: "Why is pruning important?" Without removing exhausted branches, a board full of 'a's with the word list ["aaaa...b"] explores huge useless regions repeatedly. "Return paths too?" Keep the current path in a list during DFS and copy it when a word is found. Trie Implementation 8.14
simple: Find which words from a list can be traced on a letter grid.

approaches.label: Brute Force (Word Search I for each word)
steps: For each word (skipping duplicates), try to start a DFS at every cell.
The DFS matches one character at a time, marks the cell as visited, explores 4 neighbours, then restores the cell.
approaches.why: For each of W words and each of m·n start cells, the DFS can branch 4 ways first and 3 ways after (it cannot go back), for up to L levels.
approaches.simple: Run the single-word search for each word separately.

approaches.label: Optimal (Trie of words + one DFS per cell)
steps: Insert all words into a trie; store the word string at its end node.
From each cell, dfs(i, j, parent): let node = parent.child[board[i][j]]; stop if out of bounds, visited, or node is null.
If node.word!= null, add it to the result and set it to null. Mark the cell, recurse into 4 neighbours with node, unmark.
Prune: if node now has no children and no word, remove it from parent.
approaches.time: O(m · n · 4 · 3^(L-1)) worst case, plus O(total characters) to build the trie
approaches.space: O(total characters) for the trie, O(L) recursion
approaches.why: All words are searched simultaneously, so the W factor disappears; in practice pruning makes it much faster than the bound.
approaches.simple: Put all words in a trie and explore the grid once, following the trie as you go, so shared prefixes are searched only once.

title: Trie Implementation and Advanced Operations
problem: This is Striver's "Implement Trie II" (LeetCode 1804). Implement a Trie that allows duplicates, with: insert(word), countWordsEqualTo(word) (how many times this exact word is stored), countWordsStartingWith(prefix) (how many stored words, counting duplicates, have this prefix), and erase(word) (remove one occurrence; the word is guaranteed to exist).
example: Explanation: "apple" is stored twice, then erased one at a time.
intuition: The plain trie stores yes/no information (isEnd). To answer "how many", change the flags into counters:
endCount: how many words end exactly at this node. prefixCount: how many words pass through this node (i.e. have this node's string as a prefix).

insert walks the path and increments prefixCount on every node visited and endCount on the last one. erase walks the same path and decrements the same counters. Queries walk to the node and read the right counter. Because a word passes through every node of its path, prefixCount at the prefix node is exactly the answer for countWordsStartingWith.
notes: Say it like this: "A hash map of counts handles exact words in O(L) but prefix counts need a scan of every distinct word. In a trie I keep two counters per node, how many words pass through and how many end here; insert and erase update them along the path, and both queries are a single O(L) walk."
Edge cases: erasing a word that is not present (guard it, or the counters go negative); prefix equal to a whole word ("apple" counts itself); querying a prefix whose path does not exist.

Common mistakes: incrementing prefixCount on the root (then the root counts all words, fine, but off-by-one if you read it as a prefix node); forgetting to decrement prefixCount on erase; physically deleting nodes while other words still use them.

Follow-ups: "Free memory on erase?" When a child's prefixCount drops to 0, set that link to null and stop; nothing below it is used. "Count distinct words with a prefix?" Keep a separate counter that changes only when endCount goes 0 → 1 or 1 → 0. 8.15
simple: A trie that counts: how many times a word was inserted, how many words start with a prefix, and erase.

approaches.label: Brute Force (Hash map of counts)
steps: Keep Map<String, Integer> from word to its count.
insert / erase / countWordsEqualTo are map updates and lookups. countWordsStartingWith scans every key and sums counts of keys with that prefix.
approaches.time: O(L) for insert, erase, countWordsEqualTo; O(D · L) for countWordsStartingWith, D = distinct words
approaches.why: Prefix queries must examine every distinct word.
approaches.simple: Keep a map from word to count and scan it for prefix questions.

approaches.label: Optimal (Trie with prefix and end counters)
steps: Node = next[26], prefixCount, endCount.
insert: for each character move to (or create) the child and increment its prefixCount; at the end increment endCount.
erase: walk the path decrementing prefixCount; at the end decrement endCount.
Queries: walk to the node (return 0 if the path breaks); return endCount or prefixCount.
approaches.why: One node per character on each walk.
approaches.simple: Each trie node keeps how many words pass through it and how many end there.

title: Longest Word with All Prefixes
problem: This is Striver's "Complete String" problem (LeetCode 1858, "Longest Word With All Prefixes"). Given an array of words, find the longest word such that every prefix of it is also in the array. If several have the same maximum length, return the lexicographically smallest. If there is no such word, return "" (Striver's version prints "None" instead).
example: Explanation: "apple" and "apply" both have all prefixes a, ap, app, appl present; "apple" is
lexicographically smaller. "banana" fails because "b" is missing.
intuition: "Is every prefix of this word in the set?" is a question about a path: in a trie, the prefixes of a word are exactly the nodes along its path. So the word is valid if every node on its path is marked as the end of some word. Walking a word down the trie and checking isEnd at each step answers this in O(L) instead of checking L separate substrings in a hash set (which costs O(L²) because each substring has to be built and hashed).
notes: Say it like this: "With a hash set I check all L prefixes of each word, which is O(L²) per word because each prefix is built and hashed. In a trie the prefixes are the nodes on the word's path, so a word is valid exactly when every node on its path is an end of word; that is one O(L) walk per word, O(total length) overall."
Edge cases: no valid word (return "" or "None" depending on the version); single-letter words (always valid if present); duplicates; ties in length.
Common mistakes: checking only that the path exists (it always does, the word itself created it); forgetting the lexicographic tie-break; returning the first longest instead of the smallest.

Follow-ups: "LeetCode 720 Longest Word in Dictionary?" Same problem (a word built one character at a time by other words). It can also be solved by sorting and a hash set: sort, then a word is buildable if word[0..L-1) is already marked buildable, O(Σ L log n) for the sort. 8.16
simple: Find the longest word whose every prefix is also a word in the list.

approaches.label: Brute Force (Hash set of words)
steps: Put all words in a HashSet.
For each word, check that every prefix w[0..i) for i = 1..L-1 is in the set.
Keep the best by (longer, then lexicographically smaller).
approaches.why: Each word builds and hashes L prefixes, each up to length L.
approaches.simple: Put words in a set and check every prefix of every word.

approaches.label: Optimal (Trie, check isEnd along the path)
steps: Insert every word into a trie with isEnd flags.
For each word, walk its path; if any node on the path has isEnd == false, the word is invalid.
Keep the best valid word by length, then lexicographic order.
approaches.why: Each word is inserted once and walked once; each step is O(1). (The tie-break comparison costs O(L) but only when lengths are equal, so it stays within O(Σ L).)
approaches.simple: Put words in a trie and check that every node along the word's path is a word end.

title: Number of distinct substrings in a string
problem: Given a string s, return the number of distinct non-empty substrings of s (LeetCode 1698). Striver's and GFG's version also counts the empty string, so its answer is this value + 1.
example: Explanation: The distinct substrings are a, b, ab, ba, aba, bab, abab. (Striver's version: 8, including "".)
intuition: Every substring is a prefix of some suffix: s[i..j] is a prefix of the suffix starting at i. If we insert every suffix into a trie, then every substring corresponds to a path from the root, and equal substrings share the same path. So the number of distinct substrings is exactly the number of nodes in the trie (excluding the root).

We do not even need a separate count pass: while inserting suffix i, each time we have to create a new node, we have discovered a substring never seen before, so we add 1. Trace on "abab": suffix "abab" creates 4 nodes (a, ab, aba, abab). Suffix "bab" creates 3 (b, ba, bab). Suffix "ab" creates 0 (already there). Suffix "b" creates 0. Total 7.
notes: Say it like this: "Putting every substring into a hash set is O(n³) time because each substring costs O(n) to build and hash. Every substring is a prefix of a suffix, so I insert all suffixes into a trie; each newly created node is a new distinct substring. That is O(n²) time and nodes."
Edge cases: single character (1, or 2 with the empty string); all characters equal, e.g. "aaaa" (only n distinct substrings: a, aa, aaa, aaaa); clarify whether the empty string counts.
Common mistakes: counting nodes visited instead of nodes created; forgetting the +1 in Striver's version (or adding it in LeetCode's); using substring inside the trie loop (brings back the O(n³)).

Follow-ups: "Do better than O(n²)?" Suffix array + LCP array: answer = n(n+1)/2 − Σ LCP, in O(n log n); a suffix automaton gives O(n). "Count distinct substrings of length k only?" Rolling hash in a sliding window, O(n). 8.17
simple: Count the different substrings of a string.

approaches.label: Brute Force (Hash set of all substrings)
steps: For every pair i ≤ j, add s.substring(i, j + 1) to a set.
Return the set's size.
approaches.why: There are O(n²) substrings, and creating and hashing each costs up to O(n); the set can store O(n²) strings of average length O(n).
approaches.simple: Put every substring in a set and count it.

approaches.label: Optimal (Insert all suffixes into a trie, count new nodes)
steps: For each start index i, walk from the root inserting s[i], s[i+1],... (the suffix starting at i).
Every time a child is missing, create it and increment the count.
Return the count (+1 for the empty-string version).
approaches.space: O(n²) nodes in the worst case
approaches.why: The suffixes have total length n(n+1)/2, and each character costs O(1). A string with all distinct characters creates a node for every one of them.
approaches.simple: Insert every suffix into a trie. Each new node created is one new distinct substring.

title: Maximum XOR of two numbers in an array
problem: Given an array of non-negative integers nums, return the maximum value of nums[i] XOR nums[j] over all pairs 0 ≤ i ≤ j < n (LeetCode 421).
intuition: XOR gives a 1 where bits differ. A number's value is dominated by its highest bit: having bit 30 set is worth more than all lower bits combined (2³⁰ > 2³⁰ − 1). So, for a fixed x, the best partner is found greedily from the top bit down: at each bit, prefer a partner whose bit is the opposite of x 's bit (that bit of the XOR becomes 1); only if no such partner exists, accept the same bit.

To make "does any stored number have the opposite bit here, given the bits chosen so far?" an O(1) question, store all numbers in a binary trie: each number is a path of 31 bits from bit 30 down to bit 0, each node has children 0 and 1. Querying x walks 31 steps, taking the opposite child when it exists. Trace with x = 5 (00101) against a trie holding 25 (11001): at the top bits x has 0, opposite 1 exists → XOR bits 1, 1; x has 1, 25 has 0 → 1; x has 0, 25 has 0, no other choice → 0; x has 1, 25 has 1 → 0. Result 11100 = 28.
notes: Say it like this: "Trying all pairs is O(n²). XOR is maximised greedily from the most significant bit, because one higher bit outweighs all lower bits. I put the numbers in a binary trie of 31 levels, and for each number walk down choosing the opposite bit whenever possible. That is O(32·n) time and space."
Edge cases: a single element (answer 0); all equal numbers (0); zeros; the largest value 2³¹ − 1 (needs bit 30).

Common mistakes: walking bits from low to high (greedy only works from the top); using 32 bits with 1 << 31 (negative in Java/JS) when inputs are non-negative; querying an empty trie (insert first, or start from the second element).

Follow-ups: "Without a trie?" The prefix-set method: build the answer bit by bit; for each bit, guess it is 1 and check with a hash set of prefixes whether two prefixes XOR to the guess, O(32·n). "Maximum XOR of a subarray?" Insert prefix XORs into the trie and query each prefix, O(32·n). 8.18
simple: Find the largest XOR of any two numbers in the list.

approaches.label: Brute Force (All pairs)
steps: For every pair (i, j), compute nums[i] ^ nums[j] and track the maximum.
approaches.why: n(n-1)/2 pairs, each O(1).
approaches.simple: Try every pair.

approaches.label: Optimal (Binary trie, greedy opposite bit)
steps: Insert each number into a binary trie, bits 30 down to 0.
For each number x, walk the trie from the root: at bit b, let want = 1 - bit(x, b). If that child exists, go there and set bit b of the result; otherwise go to the other child.
The answer is the maximum result over all x. (Inserting x before querying is fine: pairing with itself gives 0.)
approaches.why: Each insert and query is 31 steps; each insert creates at most 31 nodes.
approaches.simple: Store numbers bit by bit in a binary trie. For each number, walk the trie always trying the opposite bit, which makes the XOR as large as possible.

title: Maximum Xor with an element from an array
problem: Given an array nums of non-negative integers and queries [x, m], answer each query with the maximum x XOR nums[j] over all nums[j] ≤ m. If no element is ≤ m, the answer is -1 (LeetCode 1707).
intuition: Without the ≤ m limit, each query is 8.17's trie query. The limit changes which numbers are allowed for each query. Rebuilding a trie per query is too slow, but notice the allowed set only grows as m grows. So answer the queries offline in increasing order of m: sort nums, sort the queries by m (remembering their original positions), and keep a pointer into nums. Before answering a query, insert every number ≤ m that has not been inserted yet. Now the trie contains exactly the allowed numbers, and the 8.17 greedy query gives the answer. If nothing has been inserted, the answer is -1.
This "sort queries and grow the data structure" trick (offline processing) is worth remembering beyond tries.
notes: Say it like this: "Scanning the array per query is O(n·q). The allowed set only grows with m, so I process queries offline sorted by m, inserting numbers ≤ m into a binary trie as I go; each query is then the standard greedy max-XOR walk. Total O(n log n + q log q + 32(n + q))."
Edge cases: m smaller than every number (-1); several queries with the same m; x = 0; duplicates in nums.
Common mistakes: losing the original query order after sorting (store indices); returning 0 instead of -1 when the trie is empty; sorting nums but not the queries (then the pointer idea breaks).

Follow-ups: "Queries must be answered online (in the given order)?" Store in each trie node the minimum value in its subtree, and during the walk only take a child whose minimum is ≤ m; then no sorting is needed, O(32) per query. "Range of indices instead of a value limit?" Persistent trie with prefix versions.
simple: For each query (x, m), find the largest x XOR a number that is at most m.

approaches.label: Brute Force (Scan for each query)
steps: For each query [x, m], loop over all numbers, considering only those ≤ m, and track the max of x ^ num.
If none qualified, the answer is -1.
approaches.why: Every query scans the full array.
approaches.simple: For each query, scan all numbers ≤ m.

approaches.label: Optimal (Offline: sort queries by m, grow the trie)
steps: Sort nums. Create an index array of queries sorted by m.
Keep pointer p = 0. For each query in that order: while p < n and nums[p] ≤ m, insert nums[p++] into the binary trie.
If p == 0, answer -1; otherwise answer the greedy max-XOR query for x. Store it at the query's original index.
approaches.time: O(n log n + q log q + 32 · (n + q))
approaches.why: Two sorts, then each number is inserted once and each query walks 31 levels.
approaches.simple: Sort the queries by m, add numbers to a binary trie as m grows, and answer each query with the greedy opposite-bit walk.
